🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.86% (intraday, 7-year -12bp). At trading day 31 (last close) it was +0.86% against a five-campaign average of -1.07% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.70%. The 10-year is -9bp since the hike vs a +14bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 780bp against a five-year average of 415bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is holding: single-B -2bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.36 → 0.65 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+4bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,064bp, 131bp under the Oct 15 record and 612bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 81.3 (14.6%, -4.1pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 125bp, Oracle 302bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -30%, NBIS -26%, IREN -34% vs NVDA -5%.

Thursday's close was a rotation day, not a risk-off day. The S&P 500 fell 0.30% (-23.59) to 7720.39 and the Dow fell 0.25%. The Nasdaq Composite lost 1.38% (-365.13) to 26184.72, while the Russell 2000 rose 1.01% to 2859.217. The damage was concentrated: US Communication Services fell 6.6% on the day (-8.77% on the week, -14.24% on the month). Health Care (+2.5%), Real Estate (+2.25%), Cons Staples (+1.64%), Utilities (+1.56%) and Financials (+1.52%) all rose. VIX rose 1.38 to 18.58. Abroad, the Nikkei fell 2.12%, the Euro Stoxx 50 fell 1.02% and the FTSE rose 0.15%. Bonds rallied worldwide: the US 2Y fell 3.31bp to 4.5648%, the 10Y fell 3.07bp to 4.9062%, Bunds fell 3bp and JGBs fell 6.4bp. Oil went the other way, with WTI up 2.41% to 104.46 and Brent up 2.72% to 118.00. Gold fell 1.45%, silver fell 3.91% and copper fell 1.70%. The biggest credit story is HY contagion. The Caa–B gap is 780bp, well above its 5-year average of about 415bp and at the 99.7th 5-year percentile. It widened 81bp in a month and 236bp in three months, and the computed data flags it as the widest since April 2020. The FRED ICE CCC–B cross-check agrees (999bp, 99.7th percentile). So is the rot spreading upward? Not in levels yet. Single-B OAS fell 19bp on the week to 297bp, BB fell 13bp to 183bp, the B–Ba gap is at only the 41st 5-year percentile, and IG is flat on the week at 86bp. The warning sign is co-movement: the 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose from 0.36 three months ago to 0.65, though it is still just below its 0.70 five-year median. That fits CCC stress that is still idiosyncratic but starting to move more in step with single-B. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Headline US HY OAS widened 11bp to 3.23% today, which is worth watching against that backdrop. On AI credit, CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1,063.6bp. That is 611.6bp above the June low but 130.9bp below the Oct-15 record, so about 82% of the run-up is still in the price and the backstop question is unresolved. None of the AI-backstop thresholds was hit today. Sentiment: rotation plus lower yields is keeping the S&P 500 above its 50-day average, but the Nasdaq's slip below its 50-day average, $118 Brent and the CCC tail make the tape more fragile than the index level suggests.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 479.14 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD sits at 479.14 cents/gal, a 99.8th-percentile outright level (z 3.22), with the crack spread, the front-month spread and the full curve all at historical extremes at the same time. The curve is in steep backwardation, with the front 104.05 cents/gal over the 12th month and 197.8 cents/gal over the 36th. That is the shape of a very tight prompt diesel market where near-term barrels are bid far above deferred supply, not a curve-wide repricing. When the front, crack and nearby spreads have been this stretched before, those extremes have tended to ease from the front, which leans the near-term risk toward a pullback.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.77 vol points (49th percentile of the 55 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 93.5 (67th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 84bp (flatter by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (124bp above today).

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 28 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 60/100 — Inflation is sticky, not re-accelerating at the core. The underlying trimmed and median measures sit in a 2.26–2.82% band, mostly flat, and median CPI is drifting down. The pressure comes from flexible, energy-driven prices and breadth: just over half of the PCE basket is running above 3%. With Brent at 118.00, the risk is a second-round pass-through rather than a core spiral, so the Fed cannot treat 2% as close.

Today does not look like March 2000 on equity froth, but it does on credit and complacency. IG spreads (127%) and Baa–10Y (155%) are tighter than they were at the 2000 peak, but the ISM PMIs are not rolling over (9–10%). In the macro regime, the dollar is at 40% and commodities vs equities at 200% (commodities are not cheap, which is unlike 2000). Bear-market signposts are split. Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed panel describes a market whose valuations are high but not dot-com high, sitting on top of very loose credit and financial conditions. In 2000, froth sat in prices; today it sits in credit tightness and low implied volatility. That makes the CCC blow-out and the neocloud credit stress (CoreWeave CDS 1,063.6bp, CRWV equity -57.43% from its 52-week high) the more relevant bubble tell, because they show where leverage behind the AI build-out is being repriced. On the analog chart anchored at Oct-2022, the current path is at 238.3 in month 48, close to the dot-com path anchored at the Oct-1990 bear low (235.7 at month 48), whose peak came at month 113. If the analog held, that would put this cycle mid-run rather than at the top. That is a computed comparison, not a forecast. The 2000–2002 Nasdaq drawdown was -78.0% over 31 months. The analyst estimates (top-10 S&P weight of about 40%, CAPE of about 39x, market cap/GDP of about 215%, IPO froth of about 30/100, and long-term EPS growth expectations at about 65/100) were not verified by web search this run and should be treated as rough analyst estimates.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inferred: a hold is the most likely outcome at the next meeting (Dec 9 per the Guggenheim calendar). The case rests on core PCE at 3.12% and Brent at 118.00, which leave little room for a cut, combined with Warsh's stated reluctance to pre-commit. A cut becomes more plausible if payrolls stay weak (last print 29k). This is an inference, not a sourced forecast. The outcome of the Oct 28 FOMC was not verified in this run.

~1 YEAR

Inferred from his on-record views: a gradual, pre-signaled balance-sheet reduction coordinated with Treasury, toward the roughly $2.5–3T he has called appropriate (from about $6.7T), paired with a lower policy rate if inflation allows. This is a trade of rate cuts for balance-sheet reduction, which could steepen the curve through higher term premiums.

At his April 2026 confirmation hearing, Warsh told the Senate that a smaller Fed balance sheet could let rates be lower. He said reduction should be slow, deliberate, signaled in advance and coordinated with Treasury, and he declined to pre-commit to a rate path while stressing Fed independence. Commentators (PIMCO's Clarida, PNC) expect a thoughtful, framework-driven approach, and some warn that shrinking the balance sheet while cutting rates is not unambiguously easing, because term premiums could widen. With the 2s10s at about 34bp and the 30Y at 5.2772%, that term-premium risk is relevant. The search found no October 2026 Warsh speech, so the views above come from the spring record.

Sources: FXStreet – Fed chair nominee Warsh to reiterate importance of independence · PNC Economics – What to expect from a Warsh-led Fed · PIMCO – Under a Warsh Fed, expect a thoughtful policy approach · Tiger/Barron's – If Warsh becomes chair, will the Fed trade rate cuts for balance sheet reduction?
